title: Without faults, full of good
hook: one Upanishad sentence says what the self is not, then what it is, and Ramanuja keeps both halves
carry: nirguna: no faults, and an ocean of good qualities

segments.voice: Yesterday opened Vaishnava theology with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya, the book that states the other view first.
screen: `THE OTHER VIEW FIRST.` · `TODAY: WITHOUT, AND WITH.`

segments.voice: Free from evil. Free from old age. Free from death, from grief, from hunger, from thirst. That's how the Chandogya Upanishad begins describing the self worth seeking. A long run of withouts. And then, in the same breath, the sentence turns. Whose desires are real. Whose resolves come true. Suddenly there's someone there: someone who wants, and whose wanting is never empty. One sentence, two halves, a no and a yes. Some readers lean on the first half. Ramanuja says you have to keep both.
screen: `FREE FROM EVIL, AGE, DEATH, GRIEF.` → `THEN: WHOSE DESIRES ARE REAL.` → `A NO AND A YES.`

segments.voice: The Upanishads sometimes call Brahman nirguna, without qualities. Other passages pile qualities on: all-knowing, all-powerful, the source of joy. How do you read a text that seems to say both? Advaita teachers, in Shankara's line, read the withouts as the highest truth, and the qualities as true from where people stand, a lower vantage. Ramanuja, in the Sri Bhashya, reads it another way. Without qualities, he says, means without bad qualities: no evil, no decay, no limit, no lack. And the qualities the texts praise, knowledge, power, compassion, beauty, are fully real in Brahman. So the no and the yes aren't two levels. They're one portrait drawn from both sides: everything wrong ruled out, everything good affirmed. Sri Vaishnava teachers call Brahman an ocean of auspicious qualities. It's why a Vishnu devotee can recite the thousand names of Vishnu, the Vishnu Sahasranama, each name praising a quality, and not be contradicting the Upanishad at all. That's why the Chandogya sentence matters so much to him: it shows the pattern inside a single line, and neither half cancels the other. For Ramanuja, this has a human side. A God with every good quality and no flaw is someone you can bring a grief to, or sing to, as the Alvars did. His theology and their devotion meet right here. Both schools argue carefully from the same Upanishads; this is a chance to hear Ramanuja clearly, not to rank them.
screen: `NIRGUNA: WITHOUT QUALITIES.` · `WITHOUT BAD QUALITIES.` · `AN OCEAN OF GOOD QUALITIES.` · `SOMEONE YOU CAN TALK TO.`

segments.voice: If you pray, choose a few names for the One you pray to, names that each praise something good: for Vishnu, the protector, the one who is near. Before each name, quietly rule out one fear you carry about God: not cold, not far, not cruel. Then say the name, the yes. If you don't pray, do it for someone you love: set down the complaints for a few breaths, then name the good that's truly in them.
Vaishnava theology. Today, without qualities read as without bad qualities, and an ocean of good ones: a no and a yes in one portrait.
Your line: nirguna: no faults, and an ocean of good qualities. Every fault ruled out, every good thing affirmed. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas study the Sri Bhashya's reading of nirguna with a teacher, and in worship they praise Vishnu and Lakshmi through their qualities, in hymns, names and stotras that list the Lord's good qualities one by one.

fork.setup: you're Ramanuja. one Upanishad says Brahman is without qualities, another praises Brahman's knowledge and power. how do you read them together?
options: without qualities means without bad qualities; the good ones are real.
only the qualities are real; ignore the withouts.

fork.reveal: Ramanuja reads the no and the yes as one portrait: every fault ruled out, every good quality affirmed.

original.note: Sanskrit: without qualities. Ramanuja reads it as without bad qualities.

chat.meaning: Ramanuja reads nirguna as free of every fault, while knowledge, power, compassion and beauty are fully real in Brahman, so praising God's names fits the Upanishad.

tie.story: In the Sri Bhashya, Ramanuja read the Upanishad's 'without qualities' as without any fault, and praised Brahman as an ocean of good qualities.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1 (the self free from evil, age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, whose desires and resolves are real)

notes: Chandogya 8.7.1 (and 8.1.5) is paraphrased; Max Müller's 1879 SBE translation exists but the exact wording wasn't certain, so nothing is quoted.
Advaita's reading is summarized in one sentence (the qualities true from a lower vantage, vyavaharika); an Advaita reader should confirm it is fair.
Where exactly in the Sri Bhashya Ramanuja makes the 'without bad qualities' argument most clearly should be checked; references given loosely.
'Ocean of auspicious qualities' (kalyana-guna-akara) is a standard Sri Vaishnava phrase; confirm wording.
